advisor.summary: A Schedule C proprietor who uses part of the home exclusively and regularly as the principal place of business — or to meet clients, or as a separate structure — deducts the business share of home costs under §280A(c), either through Form 8829 actual expenses or the Rev. Proc. 2013-13 simplified method at $5 per square foot, capped at 300 feet. Because the deduction lands on Schedule C, it saves self-employment tax alongside income tax. The administrative-use language Congress added in 1997 superseded the Supreme Court's narrow Soliman test, so a home base for scheduling, billing, and records qualifies when no other fixed location serves that work. The model runs either method against the §280A(c)(5) income cap; exclusivity of the space — the issue exams are actually won and lost on — is file work.
mechanics: §280A(c)(1) admits three uses, each demanding exclusive and regular use: the principal place of business (including the administrative/management language when no other fixed location exists), a place for meeting patients, clients, or customers in the normal course, and a separate unattached structure.

Actual method: the business-use percentage applied to rent or mortgage interest, taxes, utilities, insurance, and repairs, plus depreciation on the office share of basis, all computed on Form 8829; direct costs of the office itself deduct in full.

Simplified method (Rev. Proc. 2013-13): $5 per square foot up to 300 square feet — a $1,500 ceiling — elected year by year on the return; no depreciation is claimed, so no unrecaptured gain builds toward a future home sale.

§280A(c)(5) caps the deduction at the business's income: it cannot create or deepen a Schedule C loss. The actual method carries the excess forward; the simplified method forfeits it — and the model applies the cap the same way.

Depreciation claimed under the actual method resurfaces at sale as unrecaptured §1250 gain, taxed at up to 25 percent and outside the §121 home-sale exclusion — the exit cost that makes the simplified method attractive for appreciating homes.

Entity owners are out of scope: after an S election the office belongs in an accountable-plan reimbursement, not on a Schedule C that no longer exists — the model declines non-Schedule-C profiles for the same reason.

authority.note: The exclusive-and-regular-use gates and the administrative/management language that prospectively superseded Soliman.
The gross-income cap: no home-office loss; carryforward under the actual method only.
The narrow principal-place test Congress overrode in 1997 — examiners still argue it for non-administrative fact patterns.
The simplified method: $5 per square foot, 300-foot cap, annual election, no depreciation, no carryover.
The actual-method computation and its expense-ordering rules.
Post-1997 depreciation is never sheltered by the home-sale exclusion — the unrecaptured-gain exit cost.

requirements: Net Schedule C profit for the deduction to land against — the income cap is real.
A measured, specific space used exclusively and regularly for the business, with photographs and a floor plan in the file.
For the principal-place prong: no other fixed location where substantial administrative work happens.
Actual method: home cost records and the square-footage computation retained.
risks: The leading audit theory is exclusivity: a guest room doubling as an office, or a desk in the family room, fails §280A's strictly construed exclusive-use test — the most commonly lost issue in this area, where photographs taken today beat testimony given later.
Actual-method depreciation builds an unrecaptured §1250 gain that survives the home-sale exclusion — clients planning to sell soon should usually take the simplified method.
The simplified method's $1,500 ceiling and no-carryover rule leave money on the table for large offices and high-cost homes — run both methods every year rather than defaulting.
Low-profit years strand the deduction against the income cap, and simplified-method excess is lost outright.
An S election silently ends the Schedule C deduction — the position must convert to an accountable plan or disappear.
stateNotes: Conformity: federal-AGI states conform automatically — the deduction arrives inside Schedule C net profit, with no separate state computation.
PTET interaction: none — a sole proprietor has no entity eligible to make a pass-through entity tax election, so there is no PTET interplay to model.
Missouri: conforms through the federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121), so the reduced Schedule C profit flows straight into the Missouri return.
reviewChecklist: Space verified as exclusively business — no dual-use furniture, no guest bed, photos on file.
Both methods computed, with the chosen method documented alongside the comparison.
Deduction tested against Schedule C profit and any carryforward tracked.
Actual-method depreciation and its exit consequences discussed with the client and acknowledged.
No conflicting claim on the same space or days under another strategy.

client.teaser: Bills you already pay every month can become a business deduction.
client.headline: Get credit at tax time for working from home
plainEnglish: If you run your business from a dedicated space at home, the tax law lets you deduct the business share of costs you already pay. Rent or mortgage interest, utilities, insurance, repairs — a slice of each can count.
The catch is the word 'dedicated.' The space must be used only for business, on a regular basis. A spare room that is truly your office qualifies. A desk in the corner of the living room does not.

There are two ways to figure it. The simple way pays $5 per square foot, up to $1,500, with almost no records. The detailed way adds up actual costs and often pays more, but it needs records and carries a small cost when you sell the home. We run both and pick the winner.
Because the deduction comes off business profit, it cuts two taxes at once: income tax and self-employment tax.
client.analogy: Your home already moonlights as your office, rent-free. This deduction makes your tax return finally recognize the rent.
benefits: Deducts a slice of costs you were paying anyway
Saves income tax and self-employment tax at the same time
Repeats every year you work from home
steps: WE confirm the space qualifies and measure it.
WE compute the deduction both ways and choose the better one.
WE file the forms with your return.
YOU keep the space business-only and snap a few photos for the file.
clientCommitments: Keep the office space strictly business-only
Tell us if you move, change the space, or form a corporation

annualMaintenance: Compare the actual and simplified methods each year with current-year costs
Confirm the space and usage still qualify; refresh photos when the office changes
deliverables: Form 8829 or the simplified election filed with the return
Home-office documentation kit (floor plan, photos, measurement record)
